title: Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL
gist: Tiger Data (formerly Timescale) released pg_vectorsearch, an alpha open-source PostgreSQL extension whose partition-based, compressed PRISM index claims a 100M-vector build in 1h40m on 128 GB vs 42 hours on 512 GB for pgvector's HNSW. Caveats: vendor-run benchmarks, no filtered search until GA, PostgreSQL 18+ only, and incremental rebalancing not yet implemented; pgvectorscale moves to maintenance mode.

insights.claim: In Tiger Data's own benchmark of 100 million vectors, the PRISM index built in 1 hour 40 minutes on a 128 GB machine, while pgvector's HNSW took 42 hours on a 512 GB machine.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Roughly 25x faster builds on a quarter of the RAM would materially cut infra cost of large vector workloads inside Postgres.
insights.quote: PRISM built an index in 1 hour and 40 minutes on a machine with 128 GB of memory, while HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) took 42 hours

insights.claim: The benchmarks are not independently validated, though they use an open-source tool, measure recall@10 against exact search and run both indexes on the same PostgreSQL configuration and instance types, with pgvector's 16-bit halfvec for HNSW.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Investors should discount vendor benchmarks until third-party replication appears.

insights.claim: PRISM replaces graph-based indexing with partitioning: it groups similar vectors into partitions stored as compressed lists densely packed into database pages, mirroring the approach of newer dedicated vector search systems.
insights.speaker: Erik Nordström, Matvey Arye, Noah Hein
insights.so_what: Brings dedicated-vector-DB-style architecture into general-purpose Postgres, eroding a differentiator of standalone vector stores.
insights.quote: PRISM groups similar vectors into partitions and stores them as a list in a compressed format that is densely packed into database pages

insights.claim: By narrowing searches to relevant partitions and scanning compressed vectors sequentially, PRISM avoids costly random memory or disk access and needs less RAM than HNSW.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Sequential-scan friendly indexes shift vector search economics from RAM-bound to cheaper storage-bound hardware.
insights.locator: While HNSW is an approximate nearest-neighbor

insights.claim: Per CTO Michael Freedman, PRISM combines hierarchical clustering, compressed vectors, RaBitQ quantization to cut distance computations, duplication of boundary vectors to improve recall, and PostgreSQL's native storage, logging and concurrency.
insights.speaker: Michael Freedman
insights.so_what: Reusing Postgres's durability and concurrency primitives lowers operational burden versus a separate vector store.

insights.claim: Incremental rebalancing is not yet implemented: centroids don't move as new vectors arrive and posting lists lose physical locality, so frequently changing data may require index rebuilds.
insights.speaker: Michael Freedman
insights.so_what: Write-heavy workloads are a weak spot today; HNSW and dedicated vector DBs retain an edge there.
insights.quote: Centroids don't automatically move when new vectors arrive, and posting lists gradually lose their original physical locality.

insights.claim: pg_vectorsearch is alpha, requires PostgreSQL 18 or later, supports up to 1968 dimensions, and will not support filtered searches combining WHERE and ORDER BY until general availability.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Lack of filtered search limits production RAG use; adoption timing hinges on GA.
insights.locator: The new vector extension requires PostgreSQL 18

themes.theme: Consolidation of vector search into Postgres

insights.claim: pg_vectorsearch works on existing pgvector columns, letting applications do vector search without a separate database.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Compatibility with pgvector lowers switching costs and strengthens the 'just use Postgres' thesis against standalone vector DB vendors.
insights.locator: According to the authors, pg_vectorsearch enables

insights.claim: Practitioner Hermon Hagos argues cheaper in-Postgres semantic search saves real money for budget-constrained RAG builders by avoiding a separate vector store or bigger server, while warning not to ship the alpha to clients.
insights.speaker: Hermon Hagos
insights.so_what: Signals demand pull from cost-sensitive RAG builders, a threat to standalone vector database pricing.
insights.quote: Fast semantic search without spinning up a separate vector store or a bigger server is real money saved.

insights.claim: Hacker News reaction was interested but cautious, questioning independent benchmark validation, whether pg_vectorsearch could replace pgvectorscale, and the lack of filtered search.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Community skepticism suggests adoption will lag until validation and GA features land.
insights.locator: In a popular Hacker News thread

insights.claim: Tiger Data plans to put its existing pgvectorscale extension into maintenance mode, consolidating its vector strategy around pg_vectorsearch.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: pgvectorscale users face a migration path; signals Tiger Data's bet on PRISM as its AI-database play.
insights.locator: The new vector extension requires PostgreSQL 18
